label: The gain shrinks downstream
title: Individual speed-ups shrink at team and company level
thesis: AI makes individual developers noticeably faster, but the gain at team and company level is much smaller. The latest large study, by NBER on more than 500,000 GitHub developers through mid-2026, finds coding activity up 240% for autonomous agents but releases up only 30%. Teams that change how they work can keep more of the gain: in an Amazon pilot, half of 50 teams reached a median 4.5 times faster delivery to production.
construct: The size of AI's measured effect on software productivity at each level (self-reported value, coding activity, task time, team throughput, releases) and the gap between those levels, including which delivery stage absorbs the difference. Not adoption rates, share of AI-written code, spend, how review assurance is done (review-shifts-to-verification), or the spread between teams with the same tools (same-tool-different-outcomes).
currentPressure: Adoption is near universal and executives expect acceleration, but organisation-level measurements show gains of roughly 2-18% in throughput and measurement practice lags.

implications.statement: Business cases and capacity plans built on task-level multipliers or self-reported savings overstate organisational gains: evidence runs from a measured -4% (METR trial) to 2-18% throughput (DORA) and 30% more releases (NBER).

Review, merge and deployment capacity absorbs part of the gain, so faster coding moves the constraint downstream: review times up 91%, 4.6x longer review waits, and git itself a bottleneck at Anthropic.
Measuring the effect is itself hard: usage leaderboards were dropped at several large companies and 26% of practitioners name productivity measurement as a top challenge.

evidence.note: NBER, 500,000+ GitHub developers: coding activity +240% for autonomous agents, +80% in projects, +30% in releases
DX, 121,000 developers: 92.6% use AI monthly, yet self-reported time savings stuck near 4 hours a week since Q2 2025; no organisation-level breakthrough (vendor study)
DORA ROI report, ~5,000 professionals: AI lifts throughput 2-18%, payoff gated by platform quality
ICSE 2026, 2,989 developers: reported time savings modest, far below marketed multipliers
Science study, ~160k GitHub developers: ~29% of US Python functions AI-written, aggregate output up ~3.6% (data to end of 2024)
Opsera benchmark, 250,000+ developers: time-to-PR down 48-58%, but AI PRs wait 4.6x longer in review and carry 15-18% more vulnerabilities (vendor benchmark)
Faros telemetry, 22,000 developers: task throughput rose, but review queues, delays and incidents grew faster
METR survey, 349 respondents: self-reported 1.4-2x value uplift; METR warns surveys overstate, its 2025 trial found developers 19% slower while feeling 20% faster
METR revised trial (57 developers, 800+ tasks): measured slowdown shrank to -4% (CI -15% to +9%); authors say magnitude of any benefit is uncertain
Reported: code review time up 91% on high-AI-adoption teams as PR throughput overwhelms reviewers
Harness, 700 engineers: among very frequent AI users 45% deploy daily or faster but 69% report persistent deployment problems
142,652 agent PRs: 27.67% hit merge conflicts, ~540 conflicting lines on average
Vendict: within a month of agents contributing at volume the constraint became review velocity (single team, weak)
37signals CTO: agents did all implementation on a new product, but established products proved much harder to accelerate (single account, weak)
Amazon Stores, 50 teams: half under 3x faster to production, the other half a median 4.5x, some over 10x; large gains do reach production where teams change how they work
2025 DORA report: AI amplifies existing engineering quality; weak foundations see instability, not gains
Pragmatic Engineer survey, 900+ developers: AI amplifies existing culture, benefits larger on strong foundations
Workday research: ~40% of AI time saved lost to rework (vendor claim, not software-specific)
BNY Mellon paper: same 2,989-developer survey as the ICSE study; output proxies miss effects, so counts of 'more shipped' mislead
Harness survey, 700 practitioners: measuring productivity (26%) and proving ROI (18%) rank among top challenges
LeadDev: token leaderboards dropped at Meta, Amazon and others; Uber's CTO says maximising tokens raised costs without improving productivity
Executive survey: 98% expect agentic AI to accelerate delivery, only 9% expect game-changing improvements
Auckland longitudinal survey, 95 matched developers: self-reported productivity flat and high while developer experience worsened
Anthropic: merged changes rose from about 2,500 to 30,000+ a day and git became the main bottleneck. Measures volume, not a productivity effect; shows pressure on downstream stages (self-reported)

Reuters from internal documents: Meta cancelled a second restructuring wave after internal data reportedly showed agents not delivering assumed gains. About restructuring, not a measured productivity effect

reachRationale: The finding is consistent across independent datasets at different scales, and few now deny that headline gains overstate what organisations see. That agreement is itself a change in what the field expects.
whatWouldChangeThis: Telemetry or controlled studies showing releases and organisation-level throughput rising roughly in step with coding activity
Replications of the DX and DORA findings showing organisation-level gains well above 20%
Evidence that gains of 4.5x or more to production, as in the stronger half of Amazon's teams, become the norm rather than the exception
Larger, less selected controlled trials showing a clear net speed-up for experienced developers
